Glass Is A Frozen Accident

materials 6 Aug 2026

Sentence29 words · 0.2 min

Glass is a liquid cooled so fast that its atoms never found their crystal — a solid keeping the disordered structure of the liquid it can no longer be.

Almost everything solid around you is a crystal: metals, salt, ice, rock, bone mineral. Their atoms sit on a repeating lattice and snap back onto it at a sharp freezing point. Glass does none of this. Cool molten silica fast enough and its tangled network of silicon-oxygen tetrahedra turns too viscous to rearrange before it can crystallise. The liquid does not freeze; it thickens, and keeps thickening, until we call it a solid. There is no freezing point — only a glass transition, a range where viscosity climbs past any practical limit and the structure locks. A window pane is a snapshot of a liquid, taken as it gave up.

Glass is a liquid cooled too quickly to crystallise, so it has no freezing point at all — and the ordinary sort is a compromise between three ingredients. Pure silica makes superb glass but melts near 1700 °C, hopeless for ancient furnaces and expensive now. Soda — sodium carbonate — breaks up the silica network and drops the working temperature by hundreds of degrees, but it drops it too far in another sense: soda-silica glass dissolves in water. Lime, from limestone, stabilises the network against water. That recipe, roughly 70% silica, 15% soda, 10% lime, has made bottles and windows for two thousand years.

Structurally, the picture is Zachariasen’s random network. Silicon sits at the centre of a tetrahedron of four oxygens, and in both quartz and glass each tetrahedron shares its corners with neighbours. The difference is only in the angles: in quartz, the bond angles between tetrahedra repeat with perfect regularity out to any distance; in glass they vary a little at random, so order persists for a couple of atomic neighbours and then dissolves. Sodium and calcium ions sit in the gaps, terminating some of the network’s bonds and making it easier to flow. The material is fully bonded and rigid, just not repetitive.

The strength story is stranger still. A silica bond is very strong, and a flawless glass fibre should withstand something like 14 gigapascals. Real window glass breaks at around a hundredth of that, because glass cannot yield. A metal blunts a crack by deforming plastically at its tip; glass has no dislocations to move, so the stress at the tip of any microscopic surface scratch concentrates until the bonds there simply part, and the crack runs at over a kilometre per second. Everything we do to strengthen glass — tempering, chemical ion exchange, keeping optical fibres pristine — is really about the surface, because glass is only ever as strong as its worst scratch.

What makes a glass a glass

The defining feature is not transparency or brittleness — plenty of glasses are opaque, and metals can be made glassy — but the absence of long-range atomic order combined with the presence of a glass transition. Cool a liquid below its melting point without letting it crystallise and you have a supercooled liquid. Keep cooling, and its viscosity climbs steeply: 10, then 10⁶, then 10¹² pascal-seconds, at which point the material takes so long to rearrange that, on any human timescale, it does not. That conventional viscosity marks the glass transition temperature, T_g. It is not a true thermodynamic phase transition but a kinetic arrest — a traffic jam, not a freeze.

Cooling rate is part of the recipe

Because the transition is kinetic, the same composition cooled at different speeds gives glasses with slightly different densities and properties. Cool slowly and the network has time to relax to a denser, lower-energy arrangement before locking; cool fast and you trap a looser one. Materials scientists capture this with the fictive temperature: the temperature at which the frozen-in structure would have been in equilibrium. Annealing — holding glass just below T_g for hours — lets stresses relax and gives a stable, uniform product. Skip it and the pane cracks on its own weeks later.

Not a slow liquid

The most persistent myth about glass is that medieval cathedral windows are thicker at the bottom because glass flows over centuries. They are uneven because crown and cylinder glass was made by spinning or blowing and was never flat, and glaziers sensibly put the heavy edge down. At room temperature the viscosity of window glass is somewhere above 10¹⁹ pascal-seconds; measurable flow would take far longer than the age of the universe. Glass is a solid. Its structure merely resembles a liquid’s.

Strength lives on the surface

Since fracture starts at surface flaws, both major strengthening methods work by putting the surface into compression, so that a crack must first be pulled open against that squeeze. Thermal tempering blasts a hot pane with cold air: the outside solidifies first, then the interior cools and contracts against an already-rigid skin, leaving the surface compressed and the core in tension. That is also why tempered glass, when it finally fails, releases its stored energy at once and dices into blunt fragments. Chemical strengthening instead soaks the glass in molten potassium nitrate at around 400 °C, swapping small sodium ions in the surface for larger potassium ones that no longer fit, wedging the surface into compression. This is what makes phone screens survivable.

And it is a very old technology

Natural glass — obsidian from fast-cooled lava, tektites from impacts, fulgurites from lightning in sand — was worked into blades long before anyone melted anything deliberately. Glassmaking appears in Mesopotamia and Egypt by around 3500 BCE, glassblowing near the Levantine coast in the first century BCE, and the modern flat pane in 1959, when Pilkington began floating a ribbon of molten glass across a bath of molten tin to produce, for the first time, a perfectly flat surface without grinding.

The failure to crystallise

Every liquid, on cooling, faces a race. Crystallisation requires that a small cluster of atoms happen to arrange itself into the ordered pattern, and that this nucleus then grow. Both nucleation and growth take time, and both are slowed by viscosity, because atoms must move to take their places.

For water, the race is easy to win: molecules are small, mobile, and reorient readily, so ice forms almost immediately below 0 °C unless you go to great lengths. For molten silica, it is nearly impossible to lose. Crystallising silica means breaking and remaking strong covalent Si–O bonds and reorienting bulky corner-shared tetrahedra into precise register. The liquid is already thousands of times more viscous than water at its melting point, and gets rapidly worse. Cool it at any rate faster than about a degree per hour and it will not crystallise at all.

The critical cooling rate defines how good a glass former a material is. Silicates: fractions of a degree per second. Common metals: on the order of a million degrees per second, achieved by splat-quenching a melt onto a spinning copper wheel, which is how the first metallic glasses were made in 1960. Certain multi-component alloys, chosen so that no crystal structure is easy to assemble from such mismatched atoms, form bulk metallic glasses at a few degrees per second, and can be cast in centimetre thicknesses.

The random network

In 1932 W.H. Zachariasen proposed the picture that still frames the subject. Glass-forming oxides, he argued, build continuous three-dimensional networks of polyhedra sharing corners, not edges or faces, with enough flexibility in the connecting angles to allow disorder without breaking the network. Silicon dioxide, boron trioxide and phosphorus pentoxide are network formers.

Other oxides cannot form a network alone, but they can break one. Sodium oxide entering silica converts bridging oxygens, shared between two silicons, into pairs of non-bridging oxygens, each attached to one silicon and balanced by a sodium ion sitting in a cavity. Every such cut increases mobility and lowers viscosity and melting point. These are network modifiers. A third class — alumina, magnesia, zinc oxide — plays either role depending on composition, and glassmakers exploit them constantly.

From those three levers comes the whole palette. Borosilicate glass replaces much of the soda with boron oxide, producing a network that expands very little on heating and so survives thermal shock: laboratory ware and oven dishes. Lead glass swaps in heavy lead ions, raising the refractive index and dispersion so that cut crystal flashes with colour, and making the melt soft and long-working. Aluminosilicates give high strength and the ion-exchange chemistry that phone covers depend on. Fused silica, with nothing added at all, gives the lowest expansion and the widest optical transmission — and demands the highest temperatures to make.

Why it breaks the way it does

A perfect glass fibre is astonishingly strong. Freshly drawn and untouched, silica fibres have been measured above 10 GPa in tension, stronger than most steels. Handle the same fibre once, and its strength falls by two orders of magnitude.

The explanation is A.A. Griffith’s, from 1920: brittle materials fail from pre-existing flaws, and the stress at the tip of a sharp flaw is amplified by roughly the square root of its length divided by its tip radius. A one-micrometre scratch with an atomically sharp tip multiplies the applied stress by a hundred. In a ductile material this concentrated stress is relieved by plastic flow — dislocations move, the tip blunts, the material yields. Glass, having no crystal lattice, has no dislocations. There is no mechanism to blunt anything. Once the bonds at the tip reach their breaking stress, the crack advances, and the geometry that concentrated the stress is preserved as it runs, up to about 1.5 km/s.

Two consequences follow. First, the strength of a glass object is a property of its surface history, not its composition, which is why glass fibres are coated with polymer the instant they are drawn. Second, glass suffers static fatigue: water molecules attack strained Si–O bonds at a crack tip, so a loaded glass part can fail hours or years after loading at a stress it initially survived. Both are engineering realities more than curiosities — they set the design rules for everything from architectural glazing to the fibre in the ground under your street.

Making it flat, and making it clear

For most of history, flat glass was a compromise. Crown glass was blown into a bubble, opened, and spun into a disc that thinned toward the rim, leaving the characteristic bullseye at the centre. Cylinder glass was blown into a long tube, cut lengthwise and flattened in a kiln. Both left a wavy surface. Plate glass, from the seventeenth century, was cast and then laboriously ground and polished flat on both sides — high quality, high cost, and enormous waste.

Alastair Pilkington’s float process replaced all of it. A continuous ribbon of molten glass at about 1100 °C is poured onto a bath of molten tin — dense enough to support the glass, molten across a wide temperature range, and kept under a reducing nitrogen-hydrogen atmosphere so it does not oxidise. Gravity and surface tension do what grinding used to: the top surface levels itself, the bottom takes the perfect flatness of the liquid tin, and the ribbon cools and is drawn off to an annealing lehr as a finished pane. Nearly every window in the world is now made this way.

Clarity is a separate battle, fought against iron. Ordinary sand contains traces of iron oxide, which gives thick float glass its familiar green edge. Low-iron sand and careful redox control produce the water-white glass used in solar panels and shopfronts. The extreme case is optical fibre: for a signal to travel 100 km, the glass must be so pure that a block of it kilometres thick would still be as transparent as a window pane. Achieving that meant abandoning melted sand altogether and depositing silica from ultrapure vapour, an idea that took attenuation from 1000 dB/km in the 1960s to 0.2 dB/km, and made the internet physically possible.

The unfinished part

For all this, the glass transition remains one of the genuinely open problems in condensed matter physics. As a liquid approaches T_g its viscosity rises by fourteen orders of magnitude over a modest temperature range, while its structure — as far as any diffraction measurement can tell — barely changes at all. Something is happening cooperatively among the molecules that we cannot yet see directly. Competing theories invoke growing regions of correlated motion, an underlying thermodynamic transition hidden below the point where measurement becomes impossible, or purely kinetic jamming with no hidden transition at all.

Philip Anderson called it the deepest and most interesting unsolved problem in solid state theory. Which is a strange thing to say about a material we have been making, by feel, since the Bronze Age.
